cases.title: The skateboarding dog

item.description: A video shows a bulldog riding a skateboard down a ramp at a park.

clues.A: The dog’s owner posted it. Her account has three years of videos of the same dog.
clues.B: A local news site ran a story about the dog last year.
clues.D: The owner names the dog and the park, and says he still falls off sometimes.
clues.E: You ask how he learned. She replies with an old video of him as a puppy, falling off.

cases.lesson: Surprising doesn’t mean fake. A long history from the same source is hard to fake.

fib.right: Ugh. I was sure you’d call a skateboarding dog fake.
fib.wrong: Ha! That dog is real. Three years of videos, and you didn’t check!

cases.title: The shark on the highway

item.description: A photo shows a shark swimming along a flooded highway. It has been shared thousands of times.

clues.A: An account called WOW Pics Daily that never says where its pictures come from.
clues.B: The same photo appears with three different city names. No news station reports a shark.
clues.C: It looks sharp and realistic. Nothing is obviously wrong.
clues.D: No. The post doesn’t say who took it or when.
clues.E: People ask “where is this?” in the comments. The account never answers.

cases.lesson: You can’t always tell by looking, and lots of shares don’t make something true.

fib.right: Fine. You got me. Three cities, one shark. Sloppy of me.
fib.wrong: Gotcha! You never checked whether anyone else saw my shark.

cases.title: The dragon drawing

item.description: A pencil drawing of a dragon is pinned to the class art wall.

clues.A: Your classmate Maya put it up.
clues.C: There are eraser marks, and one wing is bigger than the other.
clues.D: Maya says the dragon is guarding her brother’s goldfish, Bubbles.
clues.E: You ask how she made it. She shows three practice sketches in her notebook.

cases.lesson: Showing how something was made is strong proof.

fib.right: Bah. I hoped the wonky wing would throw you off.
fib.wrong: Ha! Maya drew that herself. Her sketches were right there in the notebook!

cases.title: The book summary

item.description: A study website has a summary of the book your class just finished.

clues.A: The website doesn’t name an author.
clues.B: Other summaries of the book don’t mention the big chase scene this one describes.
clues.C: The spelling and grammar are perfect.
clues.D: It describes a big chase scene. You read the book, and there is no chase.
clues.E: There’s nobody to ask. The site has no author and no contact page.
clues.F: Tiny print at the bottom says “Summaries are generated automatically.”

cases.lesson: AI can state made-up things confidently. Check against the real thing.

fib.right: Rats. I knew that chase scene was too much.
fib.wrong: Gotcha! There’s no chase in that book, and you’ve read it!

cases.title: The three hearts

item.description: A post says: “Fun fact: an octopus has three hearts.”

clues.A: The city aquarium’s official page posted it.
clues.B: An encyclopedia and a library book both say the same thing.
clues.D: The post says the keeper feeds their octopus, Pickle, at 2:00 every day.
clues.E: Someone asks why three. The keeper explains that two pump blood through the gills and one pumps it to the rest of the body.

cases.lesson: Weird doesn’t mean fake. Check a source you trust.

fib.right: Hmph. I thought three hearts sounded made up enough.
fib.wrong: Ha! It’s true. One look in an encyclopedia would have told you.

cases.title: The cousin’s voice message

item.description: A voice message sounds exactly like your cousin. He asks you to send a gift card code for a game, fast.

clues.A: It came from a number you don’t recognize.
clues.B: You call your cousin on his real number. He never sent it.
clues.C: The voice sounds exactly like him.
clues.D: It doesn’t use the nickname he always calls you.
clues.E: You text back “what’s our dog’s name?” It doesn’t answer. It just says “hurry.”

cases.lesson: Voices can be copied. Check through a way you already trust, and tell an adult. Being rushed is a warning sign.

fib.right: Ugh. One phone call to your real cousin and my whole plan falls apart.
fib.wrong: Gotcha! That was a copied voice. You should have called him back.

cases.title: The purple sunset

item.description: A photo shows a bright purple and orange sky over the beach. It looks almost too good to be real.

clues.A: Your aunt posted it. She was at that beach that evening.
clues.B: Other people in town posted the same sky that night, and so did the local weather page.
clues.C: The colors look too bright to be real.
clues.D: She says it happened right after the storm passed, around dinner time.
clues.E: You ask for more. She sends four more photos, one with her thumb over the lens.

cases.lesson: “Too good to be true” is a feeling. Other witnesses are evidence.

fib.right: Fine. The sky really did look like that. Half the town saw it.
fib.wrong: Ha! Real sunset. Everyone in town posted it, and you didn’t look!

cases.title: The friendly homework helper

item.description: A chat box on a homework website is called Sam. Sam says, “I totally get it! I had the same problem in 5th grade.”

clues.A: A chat box on the website. It only gives the name Sam.
clues.B: The site’s staff page doesn’t list anyone called Sam.
clues.C: Sam replies in one second, every time, even at midnight.
clues.D: Sam says it had the same problem in 5th grade but can’t say which school.
clues.E: You ask “Are you a person?” Sam says “I’m an AI helper.”
clues.F: Small print under the chat says “Sam is an AI helper.”

cases.lesson: AI can sound like a friend. Look for the label, or ask. It’s fine to use, as long as you know what it is.

fib.right: Bah. I can’t believe I left the label on.
fib.wrong: Gotcha! Sam’s an AI helper. All you had to do was ask.

cases.title: The five-star review

item.description: A review of a new game says: “This is an amazing game that exceeds expectations in every way. Highly recommended!”

clues.A: The account reviewed 50 different things on the same day.
clues.B: The exact same sentences appear in reviews of other games.
clues.D: It never names a level, a character, or anything that happens in the game.
clues.E: Someone asks “what’s your favorite level?” Nobody replies.

cases.lesson: Praise that could fit anything is a warning sign.

fib.right: Rats. I should have at least named a level.
fib.wrong: Gotcha! Fifty reviews in one day, and not one detail about the game.

cases.title: The hamster poem

item.description: Your friend Leo hands you a short poem about his hamster.

clues.A: Leo gave it to you himself at lunch.
clues.D: It’s about his hamster Biscuit escaping behind the fridge last week. He told you about that when it happened.
clues.E: You ask which line was hardest. He shows you his crossed-out tries at rhyming “fridge.”

cases.lesson: Mistakes alone don’t prove a person made it. Personal details and seeing the work do.

fib.right: Hmph. I was counting on those spelling mistakes to confuse you.
fib.wrong: Ha! Leo wrote that. He showed you his crossed-out lines!
